title: World
blurb: The planet and its people: seasons, time zones, languages and cities.

lessons.title: How the planet works
lessons.summary: Seasons, time zones, coordinates and the ocean's central heating.

cards.title: Why we have seasons
cards.text:
It isn't about distance: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of our winter.

Seasons come from Earth's tilt of about 23.4°. In June the northern hemisphere leans toward the Sun, so sunlight hits it more directly and days are longer. In December it leans away.

cards.title: Try it: time zones
cards.text: Earth turns 360° a day, so each hour of time difference is about 15° of longitude. Countries round that off to suit their borders, and a few, like India, use half hours. Move Lisbon's clock (winter time) and watch the world follow.

cards.title: Latitude and longitude
cards.text:
Every place on Earth has two coordinates. Latitude says how far north or south of the equator you are, from 0° to 90°. Longitude says how far east or west of the Greenwich meridian in London, from 0° to 180°.

Viana do Castelo sits at about 41.7° N, 8.8° W.

cards.title: The ocean's central heating
cards.text:
Porto and New York sit at almost the same latitude, yet Porto's winters are far milder. Part of the reason is the Gulf Stream and its extension, which carry warm tropical water north-east across the Atlantic.

Westerly winds blowing off that warm ocean bring the heat ashore. Cold water returns south, completing a vast loop.

lessons.title: People and places
lessons.summary: Who lives where, what they speak, and why cities are where they are.

cards.title: If the world were 100 people
cards.text:
About 8 billion people live on Earth; the UN marked the milestone in November 2022. Shrink that to 100 people and roughly 59 live in Asia, 18 in Africa, 9 in Europe, 8 in Latin America, 5 in North America and 1 in Oceania.

India and China alone hold more than a third of humanity. Africa is the fastest-growing region.

cards.title: The most spoken languages
cards.text:
Count everyone who speaks a language, natives and learners together, and English comes first, with Mandarin Chinese second. Count only native speakers and Mandarin leads by a long way.

Portuguese has around 260 million speakers worldwide, most of them in Brazil, which makes it the most spoken language in the southern hemisphere.

cards.title: Why cities sit on rivers and coasts
cards.text:
Before railways and roads, water was the motorway. Rivers and sheltered harbours offered drinking water, fertile soil, fish and, above all, cheap transport for trade.

That's why so many great cities stand at a river mouth or a natural harbour: Lisbon on the Tagus, Porto on the Douro, London on the Thames, Shanghai at the mouth of the Yangtze.

cards.title: How many countries are there?
cards.text:
The usual answer is 195: the 193 members of the United Nations plus two observer states, the Vatican City and Palestine. Some places, like Taiwan and Kosovo, govern themselves but aren't UN members, so counts differ.

The largest is Russia, at about 17 million km². The smallest, Vatican City, is under half a square kilometre.

quiz.q: Which region is home to most of the world's people?
quiz.explain: Roughly 59 out of every 100 people live in Asia.

quiz.q: Which language has the most native speakers?
quiz.explain: Mandarin leads on native speakers; English leads when learners are included.

quiz.q: Why did so many big cities grow on rivers and coasts?
options: Water, food and cheap transport for trade
Easier to defend from the air
quiz.explain: Water routes were the cheapest way to move goods and people for most of history.
